newsitem.title: UKRAINE: IMF official hopeful of new loan for Ukraine soon.
newsitem.headline: IMF official hopeful of new loan for Ukraine soon.

text.p: A senior International Monetary Fund official said on Saturday he was hopeful Ukraine would soon win a multi-billion-dollar long-term credit to succeed its current stand-by programme.

"If Ukraine gets the Extended Fund Facility (EFF), which hopefully they will get pretty soon, it would be a foundation for economic growth for this country," J. de Beaufort Wijnholds, IMF executive director for Ukraine and the Netherlands, said.
He was speaking to Reuters after a news conference held by members of the IMF board, in Kiev to examine the former Soviet republic's economic progress.
A separate mission is also visiting Ukraine negotiating the three-year, $2.5 to $3 billion EFF programme, which if approved would start in 1997 as the $867 million stand-by loan expires.
IMF officials have said previously that the new funding programme was expected to be decided by the end of 1996.
Ukraine has secured about $2.1 billion in IMF credits since winning approval for its market reform programme in 1994.
Wijnholds was generally positive about the economy, though he said Ukraine had to implement further structural reforms.
"By next year there is a good chance there will be positive economic growth," he said. "We think Ukraine can achieve 10 percent annual inflation in a couple of years."
The 1997 draft budget, awaiting parliamentary approval, forecasts 1.7 percent growth in gross domestic product (GDP) from a plunge of 11.8 percent in 1995.
Aimed at meeting IMF guidelines, it calls for inflation to slow to 24.9 percent from 48 percent forecast this year and a reduction in the budget deficit to 2.4 percent of GDP by Western calculations.
Wijhnholds said President Leonid Kuchma had shown a "strong commitment" to the EFF when he met the board this week.

"To improve the investment climate we need a stable environment, further liberalisation, further deregulation, and further privatisation. These requirements will be covered in the Extended Fund Facility," Wijnholds said.
Other requirements would include firmer control on government expenditures, improved tax collection and continued tight monetary policy.
He would not comment on whether Ukraine would receive a currency stabilisation fund it has requested as part of the EFF to support its new hryvnia currency, introduced in September.
The unit, introduced at 1.76 to the dollar, has gradually fallen since, reaching 1.84 by Friday.

The former Soviet republic has been criticised by international funding bodies for its slow pace of privatisation, and foreign investors frequently complain about huge bureaucratic hurdles and extremely high taxes.

Wijnholds said the EFF should help boost much-needed foreign investment, which has reached only about $1.5 billion since the country won independence in 1991. "Investors are interested but they need more confidence," he said.
